title: Netanyahu Rejects Trump's Gaza Peace Plan, Pentagon Sounds Alarm on Munitions, Syria Restructures Russian Bases
subhead: Israel's prime minister formally rejects the US-backed 15-point Gaza disarmament plan, calling it 'fictitious' and demanding full Hamas disarmament before any withdrawal. The Pentagon orders defence firms to accelerate weapons production as interceptor stockpiles shrink by up to 65 percent. Syria reaches a deal to convert Russia's military bases into joint training centres — a quiet reshaping of Moscow's footprint in the Middle East.

sections.heading: Netanyahu Rejects Trump's 15-Point Gaza Plan
sections.body:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu formally rejected the US-backed 15-point Gaza peace plan at a cabinet meeting on Sunday, declaring that Israel 'will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed'. He dismissed the framework as offering 'fictitious disarmament' and insisted on the complete surrender of all Hamas weaponry — including light arms — before any Israeli pullback from Gaza.

The rejection derails the most serious diplomatic effort to resolve the Gaza conflict since the October 2025 ceasefire. Trump's Board of Peace, established under UN Security Council Resolution 2803, had announced on July 30 that Hamas had accepted a phased disarmament process in exchange for an Israeli military withdrawal and the creation of a Palestinian National Committee to govern Gaza. Hamas reaffirmed its commitment to the plan on Sunday and called on mediators to enforce its provisions.

Netanyahu's move is inseparable from domestic politics. With Israeli elections set for October 27 and polls showing his coalition at risk, far-right ministers including Itamar Ben Gvir have pressured Netanyahu to scrap the deal entirely. Former Israeli diplomat Alon Pinkas told Al Jazeera that Netanyahu 'needs a forever war' and that the rejection 'should be viewed entirely in the context of the upcoming election'. Meanwhile, 70 percent of Jewish Israelis fear the election's integrity is at risk, according to the Israel Democracy Institute, and President Isaac Herzog has warned of violence and interference.
sections.whyItMatters: Netanyahu's rejection turns the most credible Gaza peace framework into a dead letter weeks before Israeli elections. The US invested significant political capital in this plan — its collapse would leave Gaza without any path out of the conflict and strain the US-Israel relationship further.

sections.heading: Pentagon Demands Faster Weapons Production as Stockpiles Dwindle
sections.body:
Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg sent a memo to defence industry leaders on Wednesday giving them 21 days to submit plans for 'significantly faster, more aggressive delivery schedules' on critical weapons systems. 'Years-long development cycles are not acceptable,' Feinberg wrote, according to the Washington Post. Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell confirmed the memo on Saturday, saying it would inform the fiscal year 2028 budget.

The urgency is driven by hard numbers. According to analysis by the Center for Strategic and International Studies, US Patriot interceptor stockpiles have fallen from 2,330 before the Iran conflict to between 759 and 827 — a reduction of at least 65 percent. THAAD interceptors have fallen from 452 to between 234 and 278, a 38 percent decline. Retired Marine Corps colonel Mark Cancian, a CSIS analyst, told Al Jazeera: 'If we run out of Patriots, then the missiles get through.'

President Trump again denied any munitions shortage on Thursday, writing on Truth Social that the US has 'massive amounts of munitions'. A $1.5 trillion Pentagon spending request remains stalled in Congress, where lawmakers from both parties have pushed back on the Iran war. The Pentagon recently signed new deals with Lockheed Martin and Northrop Grumman to boost production capacity, but CSIS estimates it will take at least three years to restore interceptor stockpiles to pre-war levels.
sections.whyItMatters: The US is burning through air-defence interceptors faster than it can replace them in a conflict that shows no sign of ending. A sustained shortage would force the US and its allies to ration missile defences — meaning more incoming threats get through.

sections.heading: Syria and Russia Agree to Convert Military Bases into Joint Centres
sections.body:
Syria's Foreign Ministry announced on Sunday that Moscow and Damascus have reached a memorandum of understanding on the future of Russia's two military installations in the country — Hmeimim airbase and Tartus naval base. Under the agreement, both sites will become 'joint training and capacity-building centres', with civilian facilities handed over to Damascus and a three-month deadline for the transition. Russia has not yet formally commented.

The deal is significant because these are Russia's only two official military bases outside the former Soviet Union. Since the ouster of Bashar al-Assad in 2024, Moscow has sought to preserve its Syrian foothold, with Putin meeting President Ahmed al-Sharaa twice. The agreement lets Russia maintain a presence — but on terms set by Damascus, not Moscow. Syria's foreign minister inspected both bases on Sunday, a signal of sovereignty.

The rebranding from 'military bases' to 'joint centres' is more than semantic. It reflects the reality that post-Assad Syria no longer needs Russian military support to survive, and that Moscow's regional leverage has contracted sharply. Al Jazeera's Obaida Hitto reported that Syria is using the deal to send 'a clear message that the central government in Damascus is in control of all assets that belong to Syria'.
sections.whyItMatters: Russia's last military outposts in the Middle East are being restructured on Syria's terms. This is not a full withdrawal, but it is a visible downgrading of Moscow's power projection in the region — and a signal that post-Assad Syria intends to set the terms of foreign military presence.

sections.heading: Typhoon Dolphin Forces Over One Million From Homes in China
sections.body:
Typhoon Dolphin made landfall in China's Zhejiang province on Sunday evening with winds of 150km/h (94mph), striking first near Yuhuan before hitting Wenzhou about an hour later. More than one million people were evacuated, 1,400 flights were cancelled in Shanghai alone, and authorities issued their highest-level red alert before downgrading the storm to a tropical storm on Monday morning. Heavy rain and flooding risks extend through Wednesday across seven provinces, including Shandong, Henan, and Hubei.

Shanghai Disneyland and Legoland closed, along with Bund viewing platforms. Dolphin is the most powerful tropical cyclone to hit China this year. No fatalities have been reported so far, but the full impact on infrastructure and agriculture will take days to assess as the storm moves inland.
sections.whyItMatters: A million-person evacuation and major transport disruption in China's economic heartland is a significant logistical event. The storm's impact on supply chains and agriculture in eastern China could compound existing economic pressures.

sections.heading: Houthis Escalate Attacks on Yemen's Al-Makha and Saudi Refinery
sections.body:
Houthi forces launched two waves of missile and drone attacks on the Red Sea port city of al-Makha in less than 24 hours, killing at least 11 people — including eight military personnel and three civilians — and wounding 32. Government forces said they intercepted six drones and two ballistic missiles during the second wave, while an unmanned explosive boat approaching the commercial port was destroyed. The Houthis said the operation targeted Saudi troop concentrations and weapons depots.

Separately, the Houthis claimed a drone strike on a Saudi Aramco refinery in Jizan. Saudi Arabia confirmed a fire was extinguished without casualties but did not identify the cause. The attacks come one day after the Saudi-Pakistan-Turkey defence pact was signed in Mecca — a pact that all three signatories insisted was not directed at Iran, but which the Houthis' escalation now directly tests.
sections.whyItMatters: The Houthi escalation is a direct challenge to the new Mecca defence pact's credibility. If the three powers cannot protect their own territory and allies from Houthi strikes, the pact's deterrent value erodes before it takes effect.

sections.heading: Around the World: Drones Over German Base, BC Wildfire, AOC Signals Ambition
sections.body:
Two drones were spotted over a German military base at Mechernich near Bonn that reportedly houses Patriot missile system components — just days after an explosive-laden drone was found on the runway at Leipzig/Halle airport. German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told Bild: 'We're not at war, but we are the daily target of hybrid warfare.' Suspicion has fallen on Russia, which denies involvement.

In British Columbia, the Bald Range wildfire has grown to 136 sq km (53 sq miles), forcing more than 20,000 people from their homes in Summerland, Peachland, and surrounding areas. BC Premier David Eby said one fire official likened the blaze to 'a bomb going off'. The state of emergency covers the Okanagan region.

US Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez revealed she is freezing her eggs and told ABC News she has not 'ruled out' a presidential run, adding that 'anything was possible' when asked about a potential 2028 Senate challenge to Chuck Schumer. The comments come ahead of November's midterm elections.
sections.whyItMatters: The drone incidents in Germany are part of an escalating campaign of sabotage and intimidation across Europe that NATO has not yet figured out how to counter. The BC wildfire underscores another summer of climate-driven displacement in North America.

bottomLine: Netanyahu's rejection of the Gaza peace plan is the day's most consequential development — it kills the only diplomatic framework for ending the war in Gaza, weeks before Israeli elections where his coalition is under pressure from the right. The Pentagon's admission that interceptor stockpiles have fallen by up to 65 percent underscores that the Iran conflict is consuming US military capacity faster than it can be rebuilt. Syria's restructuring of Russia's bases marks a quiet but real contraction of Moscow's Middle East presence. And Houthi strikes on al-Makha and a Saudi refinery immediately test the credibility of the newly signed Mecca defence pact.
